about: Reference answers to some of the fixture's questions, written from its pages: each claim cites the page it is on, the numbers and the quotation are the pages' own, and an uncovered question is said to be uncovered. `brain eval --answers eval/answers.json` scores their citations; the tests hold `brain ground` to finding nothing wrong in them.
q01: Memory for newly learned material drops fast at first and then more slowly [[forgetting-curve]]. Ebbinghaus measured it on himself in 1885, testing lists of nonsense syllables after delays of up to a month: retention "falls steeply in the first hour after learning and then levels off" [[ebbinghaus-1885]].
q03: It depends on how long the material must be kept [[spacing-effect]]. A meta-analysis of 317 experiments puts the best gap at roughly 10 to 20 percent of the retention interval, so a test a year away wants sessions about a month apart [[cepeda-2006]].
q04: Yes, over time. Students who took practice tests remembered more of a passage after one week than students who reread it, although rereading did better on a test five minutes later [[roediger-karpicke-2006]]. Pulling an answer out of memory strengthens it more than reading it again [[testing-effect]].
q05: SuperMemo schedules reviews by the SM-2 rule [[supermemo]]. Each card's interval grows after every successful review, multiplied by its ease factor, which starts at 2.5; answers are graded from 0 to 5, a grade below 3 resets the card to an interval of one day, and the first two intervals are fixed at 1 and 6 days [[wozniak-sm2]].
q09: A per-card multiplier for the next review interval: it starts at 2.5 and drops when answers are graded hard [[wozniak-sm2]].
q11: Relearning a list takes less time than learning it did; the time saved, which Ebbinghaus called savings, measures what was retained [[ebbinghaus-1885]].
